title: Costco Barely Profits From Its Products. So How Does It Make $9 Billion?

shorts.title: Costco barely profits from the stuff it sells
shorts.headline: Costco's profit isn't in the shopping cart
shorts.narration: Costco sold two hundred ninety seven billion dollars of merchandise last year. Groceries, tires, televisions, gas. And it kept a gross margin of only about eleven percent, far below a normal retailer. So where does the profit come from? Membership fees. Five point nine billion dollars of them. That one line is equal to about sixty four percent of Costco's entire net income. Costco isn't really a store. It's a club that happens to sell groceries.

shorts.title: Why Costco's $1.50 hot dog never gets more expensive
shorts.headline: The hot dog that hasn't changed price since the 80s
shorts.narration: A hot dog and a soda at Costco still cost one dollar fifty, the same price as in the nineteen eighties. Inflation should have pushed it far higher. So why doesn't Costco raise it? Because the hot dog isn't the product. You are. Costco makes its money when you renew your membership, and in the US and Canada, about ninety two percent of members do, every single year. A cheap hot dog is a tiny cost to keep that habit alive.

shorts.title: 84 million people pay Costco before buying anything
shorts.headline: 84 million people pay Costco just to walk in
shorts.narration: Before you buy a single thing at Costco, you pay. Eighty four point one million paid members did that in fiscal twenty twenty six, up from seventy six point two million two years earlier. On average, each one pays about seventy dollars a year. And here's the trick: Costco can price everything else close to cost, because the fee is almost pure profit. When the US basic fee went from sixty to sixty five dollars, members barely blinked.
